newsitem.title: UK: Analysts laud ICI sale, split over stock.
newsitem.headline: Analysts laud ICI sale, split over stock.

text.p: Analysts united on Monday in praising the value achieved by Britain's Imperial Chemicals Industries Plc in its $3 billion sale of polyester and Tioxide businesses to DuPont Co.
However they said ICI still had much to do in the way of disposals, and continued to be split over the fair value of shares in the newly-transformed company.
The speed with which ICI's oft-criticised management team achieved its sale to DuPont and the prices obtained surprised many observers.

"They have handled this much better than they have done anything in the past," said Williams de Broe analyst Peter Cartwright. "We have always been critical in the past because they have been so inward looking."

Analysts said the average price of 1.4 times sales for the businesses was highly creditable. Some analysts had predicted a price for the polymer business as low as 0.3 times sales, compared with two times sales actually paid.
"They have done very well here," said Kleinwort Benson analyst Michael Eastwood. "They have generated good returns for ICI -- 1.4 is much better than the market was expecting."
However analysts said there was still much to do on disposals and rationalisation of the new-look operation.
Nikko Europe's Philip Morrish told Reuters Financial Television "ICI can't stop here. It has to carry on the portfolio changes."

Top of the list will be the North American Tioxide business, which ICI said it hoped to dispose of within the next nine months. Other candidates for sale include the fertiliser, chlor chemical and explosives operations, with managers targeting completion in the next 12 months.

De Broe's Cartwright said the prices paid by DuPont did not indicate the levels that would be achieved for the remaining operations. He said DuPont had paid a premium for ICI's polyester and Tioxide businesses because they hoped to become a major player in the sector, reducing fragmentation and "imposing some discipline."
"DuPont's was a strategic buy of strategic assets," said Cartwright.
The sale, which will help fund the $8 billion acquisition of Unilever Plc's specialty chemicals business announced in May, means analysts will have to rip up their forecasts for the group's earnings.
Kleinwort Benson's Eastwood said the sale would have an immediate beneficial impact on interest charges, although not on operating profits.
Earnings per share are, however, expected to pick up quickly, reflecting the higher quality earnings of the newly acquired Unilever businesses.
"If you take out commodities, all margins are growing," said Morrish.

Cartwright said he expected 1998 earnings per share (EPS) of "at least 60 pence." According to Edinburgh Financial Publishing, the most recent consensus among analysts was for 1998 EPS of 56.8 pence, already well ahead of the 40.1 pence predicted for 1997.
However, analysts are split over the continued escalation in the value of ICI's shares, which jumped 75 pence to 885-1/2 pence in mid-afternoon trade, with U.S. buyers said to be particularly active.
Nikko's Morrish said the shares could rise to between 9.50 stg and 10 stg per share. "We'll probably see it in the next few weeks," he added.
However, Kleinwort Benson's Eastwood retains his sell stance on the stock, which he said "has gone to far". He said around eight stg per share would be fair value.

ICI is currently on the most demanding price/earnings ratio for the current year in its sector according to Reuters 3000 data, with a prospective PE of 20.21 times 1997 earnings based on the business before the DuPont sale. This puts it ahead of BOC Group Plc on 17.71. On a 1998 basis it slips to second place behind BOC, on 16.05 and 14.35 times earnings respectively.
